extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students and researchers interested in humour/humor
extracted.subtask_description: Summarize theories, components, styles, methods, social functions and empirical findings about humour for a general/academic audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of humour
rubrics_metrics.description: Humour (Commonwealth English) or humor (American English) is the tendency of experiences to provoke laughter and provide amusement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as the basic delimitation of the subject: things that provoke laughter or amusement fall under 'humour'. The article notes this is ultimately subjective and influenced by many variables.

rubrics_metrics.name: Benign-violation theory
rubrics_metrics.description: Humour only occurs when something seems wrong, unsettling, or threatening, but simultaneously seems okay, acceptable or safe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presented as a prevailing account (attributed to Peter McGraw) explaining when violations become funny: they must be both a violation and benign/acceptable. Use this to evaluate whether an instance of possible humour meets the 'benign violation' condition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theoretical families (psychological, spiritual, mystical)
rubrics_metrics.description: Many theories attempt to account for humour's existence, including psychological theories (which often view humour as healthy), spiritual theories (humour as a 'gift from God'), and mystical views that treat humour as unexplainable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analysing humour, situate explanations within these families—e.g., psychological accounts focus on functions and effects, spiritual accounts on value, mystical on ineffability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sociological factors affecting humour reception
rubrics_metrics.description: Acceptance of a particular style or incidence of humour depends on sociological factors and varies between people and cultures; variables include geographical location, culture, maturity, level of education, intelligence and context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate humour with attention to audience demographics and social context; what is funny in one culture or age group may not be in another. Consider examples (slapstick for children vs satire for mature audiences).

rubrics_metrics.name: Humour styles (adaptive vs maladaptive; four styles)
rubrics_metrics.description: Two types: adaptive (facilitative/affiliative and self-enhancing) and maladaptive (self-defeating and aggressive). Affiliative humour amuses others and reduces tension; self-enhancing uses a humorous perspective to cope; aggressive includes sarcasm and disparagement; self-defeating uses self-disparagement to amuse others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these style distinctions to judge psychological/social impacts: adaptive styles associate with better wellbeing, maladaptive with poorer wellbeing. Examples and research findings are provided linking styles to outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Psychological well-being criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: High levels of adaptive humour (affiliative and self-enhancing) are associated with better self-esteem, positive affect, greater self-competency, anxiety control and improved social interactions; maladaptive humour is associated with anxiety and depression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing humour interventions or an individual's humour use, consider which humour style predominates and its likely effects on wellbeing; research evidence cited supports these associations but notes some studies do not fully support causation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physiological effects and mixed evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Humour and laughter have been linked to increased pain tolerance and transient increases in SIgA (immune marker), but other physiological claims (cardiovascular benefits, sustained muscle tone effects, oxygen saturation changes) have mixed or null findings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat physiological benefit claims cautiously: cite experimental setups (e.g., cold pressor test) and note inconsistent evidence and study limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laughter ≠ humour (differentiation of emotions in laughter)
rubrics_metrics.description: Laughter and humour do not always have a one-to-one association; different laughter types can correlate with different emotions (joy, tickle, schadenfreude, taunt) and recognition rates vary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume laughter always signals positive humour; consider behavioural and emotional context and empirical findings that differentiate laughter types.

rubrics_metrics.name: Root components of humour
rubrics_metrics.description: Humour's root components include being reflective of or imitative of reality; surprise/misdirection; contradiction/paradox; and ambiguity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these components as analytic primitives when constructing or evaluating humour: e.g., does the piece create surprise or exploit ambiguity? The article also frames 'surprise' explicitly as a component of humour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humour methods/devices
rubrics_metrics.description: Common methods include farce, hyperbole, metaphor, pun, reframing, self-deprecation, timing, and manipulation of behaviour/place/size.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat these as concrete techniques available to practitioners; examples are scattered through the article (e.g., sight gags fitting behaviour/place/size categories). Use them to classify jokes or comedic passages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rowan Atkinson's three ways to make an object/person funny
rubrics_metrics.description: An object or a person can become funny by (1) behaving in an unusual way, (2) being in an unusual place, or (3) being the wrong size.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This simple heuristic is useful for visual/sight-gag comedy: check whether the target deviates in behaviour, location, or scale to produce humour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exaggeration as a universal comic device
rubrics_metrics.description: Exaggeration (taking salient traits to the point of absurdity) is considered by some theoreticians to be a universal comic device, taking different forms across genres.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating comedic effectiveness, check whether exaggeration highlights salient traits to absurdity; appropriate exaggeration varies by genre and audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taxonomy of humour genres and categories
rubrics_metrics.description: A taxonomy used (e.g., for classifying humorous tweets) includes: Anecdotes, Fantasy, Insult, Irony, Jokes, Observational, Quote, Role play, Self-deprecation, Vulgarity, Word play, Other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this taxonomy to classify humorous content by genre; helpful for annotation, automated classification, and comparative analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultural variation and translation sensitivity
rubrics_metrics.description: Different cultures have different typical expectations of humour and comedy shows may not travel well; translation mistakes and cultural norms (e.g., attitudes toward irony, religious sensitivities) shape what is acceptable or funny.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess humour for cross-cultural portability and sensitivity; examples include Confucian/Chinese historical attitudes and media observations about irony across British/American/German audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social transformation model of humour
rubrics_metrics.description: This model links the humorist, audience, and subject matter, proposing that humour transforms the subject matter and alters audience perception of the humorist, e.g., deliberate self-deprecating humour can communicate a desire for acceptance and may increase romantic attraction under favourable conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this model to understand strategic uses of humour (e.g., self-deprecation to signal affiliative intent) and to evaluate social effects on relationships and impression management.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate use of humour in the workplace
rubrics_metrics.description: Workplace humour can relieve boredom, build relationships and camaraderie, reduce tension, act as a coping strategy, improve mood and creativity, mitigate authoritative tone (e.g., managerial self-deprecation), and be managed for organisational goals (e.g., 'workplay').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate workplace humour for its social functions and risks: appropriate, shared humour can boost morale and creativity, but must be managed to avoid undermining performance or offending employees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humour in education and youth social development
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of humour plays an important role in youth peer interactions, conflict resolution, school success and psychological adjustment; socially acceptable humour lowers likelihood of being bullied while self-disparaging humour raises it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging humour among children/adolescents, prioritise social acceptability and consider potential risks (self-disparagement leading to victimisation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of humour as coping/mechanism (therapeutic boundaries)
rubrics_metrics.description: Humour can attenuate negative emotions and serve as escapist coping for momentary stress; however, it may be less effective for stronger negative stimuli and some interventions (e.g., humour-based treatments for schizophrenia) have uncertain effectiveness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply humour-based interventions with caution and empirical grounding; consider intensity of negative affect and that humour may help short-term distress but not replace other therapeutic approaches for severe issues.
